book: 088 - Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later

chapters.relation: The introduction argues that Justified grips its audience because nothing in it is black-and-white: even Mags Bennett has some good in her, even Art gives Raylan a black eye, and Harlan's crime is bred by coal-industry exploitation while religion (Billy St. Cyr's Last Chance Salvation Church, Boyd's born-again congregation of ex-cons) may be salvation or a grift. Its central example is the pilot's Miami rooftop scene, where Raylan gives hitman Tommy Bucks twenty-four hours to leave town and then kills him when the clock runs out, raising the question the whole book pursues: is Raylan justified, or is it murder dressed up as cleaning up Harlan County? It closes by previewing the book's essays in ethics, political philosophy, epistemology, metaphysics, and logic.

The chapter argues Boyd Crowder personifies coolness - composure, wily cleverness, unconventionality, intelligence, likability - as shown in the 'Cottonmouth' payroll-robbery scene where he turns his flip phone into a room bug, overhears Kyle planning to blow him up in the mine, and lets the plotters kill themselves. Jon Cotton borrows Wittgenstein's family-resemblance model to define coolness as an indefinable cluster of traits (with Dewey Crowe as the agreed uncool case), and reaches back to Socrates' defining of ethical virtues and the Republic's just, well-ordered soul to argue that coolness is a genuine ethical virtue - the excellence of a properly functioning person - in a scientific, post-religious ethics.

The chapter juxtaposes the 1992 no-knock raid in which 84-year-old paraplegic Annie Rae Dixon was shot in her bed with Raylan's pilot-episode ultimatum to Tommy Bucks, arguing both deaths count as 'justified' only because aggressive proactive policing manufactured the lethal encounter. It catalogues Raylan's tactics - provoking draws, kidnapping the cartel chief's niece and Dickie Bennett, the lucky-sniper standoff at the Bennett compound - and asks whether we want our police to be judge, jury, and executioner. On the deontological approach Raylan's routine lawbreaking cannot be justified whatever the results, and even on the consequentialist approach the war-on-drugs data (soaring murder rates in targeted neighborhoods, mass incarceration) suggest proactive policing fails on its own terms.

The chapter argues coal made Boyd Crowder possible: company scrip, Bloody Harlan's union-busting terror, black lung (Boyd's would-be assassin takes the bridge job because mining ruined his lungs), and Black Pike's mountaintop removal leave Harlan no viable work outside the mines, so crime is the rational alternative. It reads this through Hegel's 'rabble' from the Philosophy of Right - civil society is never wealthy enough to prevent an excess of poverty, and the rabble loses the honor of self-support - plus Marcuse's affluent-society critique of an existence that 'violently defends its own servitude'. Boyd's outlawry, which sets its own code above mere criminality, is a rebellion against being pushed into the rabble, and Hegel's remedy of emigration explains why leaving Harlan is the only escape, though the coal train hauls coal out while the people stay.

The chapter applies Critical Race Theory - Derrick Bell's theses that racism is ordinary and structural, advances white interests (interest convergence, illustrated by his reading of Brown v. Board), and that race is socially constructed - to argue Justified reinforces white superiority. Its Black characters are overwhelmingly criminals (bookie Arnold Pinter, enforcer Curtis Mims, bail jumper Jody Adair, drug-dealing butcher Ellstin Limehouse, who disciplines Bernard with the lye pit), law enforcement is white, and even the positive Rachel Brooks remains a bit-part mystery. Following media research on differential racialization and the cumulative effect of TV portrayals, it concludes the show is one more vehicle teaching viewers that whites keep African Americans in line.

The chapter turns Raylan's claim that shooting Tommy Bucks was 'justified' into a question of epistemic justification, expounding Plato's Meno definition of knowledge as justified true belief, Gettier's 1963 counterexamples (rebuilt with Boyd truly but luckily predicting that a marshal will be arrested), and the repairs of Goldman's no-false-causal-link condition and Harman's inference to the best explanation. It then grades the show's reasoners: Raylan knows the Crowes rather than Boyd killed Wade Messer, Boyd knows Cassie milks the revival snakes' venom, Art Mullen does not yet know Raylan helped Winona return the evidence-room money, and gut-feeling victims like Ellen May do not know what they saw. Against Humean skepticism about cause and effect it defends inductive, detective-style knowledge - Raylan can know who done it without courtroom proof.

The chapter asks whether Boyd's survival of Raylan's bullet in the premiere was a genuine sign from God: the atheist invokes Ockham's Razor and the promise of a naturalistic explanation, while the theist replies that a world-creating God would act through the laws of nature, making such explanations neutral rather than negative evidence. It then applies William James's pragmatist standard from his study of mystical experience - judge the sign by the fruits of the Spirit (Galatians' love, joy, peace, self-control) it bears - to Boyd's prison ministry, his urging Raylan to forgive Arlo, and his meth-lab crusade. Despite Boyd's eventual apostasy after Bo murders his congregation, the author concludes he passes James's test, since faith is a maintained journey that can be lost, and the born-again Boyd still struggles - like Jacob becoming Israel - rather than scheming coldly.

The chapter reads preacher Billy St. Cyr's snake-handling through Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling: like Abraham, Billy performs the absurd double movement - fully resigning himself to dying by rattlesnake while believing he will be spared - which is why Boyd Crowder, who abandoned faith for Hegel's objective rational certainty, can neither buy him out nor understand him. Kierkegaard's teleological suspension of the ethical explains why Billy and Abraham may set obedience to God above self-preservation and social morality, while Boyd's showdown in 'Truth and Consequences', where he hands Billy an un-milked rattlesnake, exposes that Billy's certainty has curdled into the hubris de Silentio warns against, so Billy is no Abraham. De Silentio's three marks - love, humility, no desire to instruct others - separate genuine faith from cult leaders and violent extremists.

Cast as a pub dialogue between philosopher Christian Cotton and therapist Anthony Palazzo over Ava Crowder's killing of her abusive husband Bowman at supper, the chapter asks when extra-legal violence is morally justified. It explains her entrapment through systems theory - homeostasis, learned helplessness, self-esteem destruction, false hope - and takes up Kant's debt metaphor for punishment, on which wrongdoers owe a penalty and retribution restores balance, to ask who may collect when the legal system treats domestic violence as a 'family matter'. They conclude Bowman did not strictly deserve death, but Ava's 'I did what I had to do' is best understood as acting from anger in pursuit of justice and self-reclamation rather than on anger for vengeance.

The chapter maps the Raylan-Boyd rivalry onto two ethical theories: Raylan is a Kant-style deontologist who does his duty (tracking Tommy Bucks to Miami, weighing duty to the law against duty to Arlo, giving every opponent the choice to walk away), while Boyd is a Mill-style consequentialist maximizing good for himself and Ava, whose vigilante church and revenge plots follow from outcomes rather than rules. Their season-one team-up against Bo Crowder and the Miami shooters is read as contractarianism, two moral agents cooperating toward a right. Each man's choices become his undoing - Raylan's damsel-saving affairs, Mags's family loyalty, Dewey's impulsiveness - which the chapter takes as the show's thesis that what we do results in who we are.

The chapter argues the show's refrain 'He pulled first; I was justified' never closes the question, using J.L. Austin's 'A Plea for Excuses' distinction between justifying an act (admitting it happened but denying it was bad) and excusing it (accepting it was bad but denying responsibility) - a line Raylan himself blurs when he confesses to Winona he may have wanted revenge for what Tommy did in Nicaragua. It deploys Austin's performatives from How to Do Things with Words on the pilot's rooftop scene: Tommy treats Raylan's countdown and dinner-chat as failed speech acts lacking authority and uptake ('supreme bullshit'), and Boyd's 'God made me do it' defense of the meth-lab bombing is likewise just an excuse, as Art's thrown Bible insists. Judge Reardon's collapse into a gray case, Ava's manslaughter plea, and Roland Pike's faith that kindness and retribution are systemically owed round out the claim that in a performative world justification is an impossible standard.

The chapter transplants Edward Said's Orientalism to Appalachia as 'Appalachianism': reality shows like Here Comes Honey Boo Boo and Mountain Monsters, and the hillbilly-redneck archetype, construct the region's people as ignorant savages so their land can be strip-mined 'for their own good' - the same logic by which colonizers claimed the Orient needed civilizing. Mags Bennett becomes the subaltern given voice, her 'The Spoil' speech about slurry impoundments and poisoned valleys speaking for generations of Appalachian women, while Boyd's taunt to Detroit's Robert Quarles - 'You're a conquistador... Only, we are not your savages' - names the colonial dynamic outright. The chapter contends that Appalachianism hides the contest for coal behind our amusement at 'those people', and that the show mostly reproduces the stereotype it occasionally resists.

The chapter surveys Harlan's gendered violence - Ava's killing of Bowman, the routine roughing-up of Audrey's working girls, Robert Quarles's childhood prostitution - and uses Catharine MacKinnon's account of patriarchal power imbalance to explain victim-blaming, underreporting, and police disbelief of trauma responses in domestic-violence and rape cases. On prostitution it weighs sex-positive feminism against the objectification worry, concluding via Teri's line about 'sucking hillbilly dicks for money' that Audrey's women have little real choice even under Ava's management. Finally it brings in bell hooks's third-wave point that oppression cannot be split from race and class, plus Peggy McIntosh's invisible backpack of white privilege, to read Noble's Holler's isolation and the bombed black church as evidence that patriarchy in Justified is always also racial and economic.

The chapter argues Justified populates both sides of the law with failed patriarchs: Arlo beats his wife and son, sets Raylan up at Bo's motel, replaces Raylan with surrogate son Boyd (and dies shooting at the man he wrongly thinks threatens him); Bo hangs Boyd's congregation as 'Crowder gospel'; Theo Tonin passes over Robert Quarles for his biological son Sammy, creating a monster who in turn phones his own ignored son beside a bound hostage; and Raylan grows into a deadbeat dad who Skypes his daughter from Harlan. Reading the fathers in the Freudian terms borrowed from film scholar Janet Walker - the father as the son's potential killer - it shows only Art Mullen does the work of a real father, repeatedly rescuing, forgiving, and finally punching the son who disappoints him, making the show a baroque inversion of the Western's promised happy family.

The chapter reads season two's families through Engels's Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State: Mags performs the patriarch's role of accumulating and bequeathing wealth (the Black Pike payout 'sufficient to provide for my kin for generations'), Arlo fails it by hoarding nothing for Raylan, and Ava joins Boyd's crime precisely when he hands her the mine money for her mortgage - a moment the author calls borderline prostitution, as Engels predicts. Hegel's Philosophy of Right, where the family exists for love and for forming free moral beings who must leave it, exposes the Bennetts' failure on both counts, while Aristotle's Politics (the polis is prior to the family) and Plato's Republic (rulers without private families, children raised in common) ground the claim that feuding clans need the state. The Kentucky-fried twist: when government and coal companies treat mountain families as spoil, family is sometimes all you've got.

The chapter reads Harlan's family bonds through Freud's Oedipus Complex - Raylan bails Arlo out only at stepmother Helen's request, and Coover whimpers 'I'm sorry, Mamma' while cradled in Mags's arms after she hammers his hand, the submissive son destroyed by his need for his mother's approval. It then applies Schopenhauer's pessimism to Winona's pregnancy: if life is suffering, as On the Vanity of Existence argues, bringing a child into Harlan is selfish vanity, and Mags's dynasty-building - grooming Loretta, bequeathing the weed business - is the will-to-live seeking immortality through the family name. Only Boyd and Ava's unsentimental care for the demented Arlo, the chapter suggests, escapes both the Oedipal trap and the vanity of lineage.

The chapter argues Ava Crowder lives by hedonism - from Aristippus's pursuit of pleasure to Bentham's utilitarianism - with Bentham's censorial principle (weighing everyone's happiness) stripped out: she kisses Raylan moments after shooting Bowman, takes over Audrey's, orders the murder of Ellen May, and in Season Five has Penny dislocate her arm for infirmary access, kills Judith in the chapel, and finally informs on Boyd to Raylan for her own release. Bentham's seven-dimension hedonic calculus (intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity, fecundity, purity, extent) supplies the framework for each choice, and the verdict is that Ava's pleasure-maximizing left her directly or indirectly responsible for three deaths - which, for her, is all that matters.

The chapter argues Mags Bennett is the show's 'outlaw mother', read through feminist media theory: she escapes Laura Mulvey's male gaze as an unkempt older woman viewers are never invited to look at pleasurably, defies the institution of motherhood described by Adrienne Rich (hammering Coover's hand as tough love), and literalizes Andrea O'Reilly's outlaw mothering - questioning the 'shoulds' of motherhood and not always putting children first. Stuart Hall's encoding/decoding model explains how audiences can hold her simultaneously as the poisoned-apple-pie murderer of Walt McCready and the maternal folk hero of the whoop-de-do. Her Black Pike reversal - the community speech followed by selling out the mountain for Doyle's sons - seals the portrait of a mother whose love is indistinguishable from strategy.

The chapter diagnoses Raylan with Aristotle's akrasia (lack of self-restraint): Art's 'lost cause' lecture, Arlo's boast that he has never shot anyone, and Boyd's 'you wake up in the morning pretending that you are not the bad guy' all charge him with acting on passion against his own calculations - sleeping with witness Ava, resuming adultery with Winona when her ring comes off. Because Raylan feels regret, the Aristotelian mark of the unselfrestrained person who knows his condition, he is curable and lacks self-restraint by habit rather than nature (Nicky Augustine's limo verdict: 'it's not who you are'). The chapter reads Raylan's signature move - forcing men to draw first so their deaths count as justified - as a perversion of justice by an akratic who is not wicked, and the series arc as his slow acquisition of self-restraint.

The chapter assembles real contested self-defense cases beside Raylan's shooting of Tommy Bucks - the OK Corral and Wyatt Earp's far-from-clean vendetta ride, Curtis Reeves killing a texting moviegoer over thrown popcorn, George Zimmerman and Trayvon Martin, Ossian Sweet's mobbed house, Bernie Goetz's subway shooting, Gary Plauche executing his son's abuser on camera, and the Texas father who beat his daughter's rapist to death. Its philosophical machinery is Aquinas's principle of double effect from the Summa Theologica (self-defense may have two effects, saving one's life and slaying the aggressor, only the first intended), set against St. Augustine's condemnation of private self-defense as inordinate self-love. Florida's stand-your-ground law - where the dead man cannot tell his side - supplies the legal gray zone the show's title exploits.

holes.name: Family Resemblance
holes.what: Wittgenstein's idea that many concepts are united not by a common essence but by overlapping, criss-crossing similarities, like the faces of one extended family.
holes.why: Chapter 9 uses family resemblance as its central tool to argue 'coolness' (Boyd Crowder) is a cluster concept that cannot be defined by a single essence, and no taxonomy slug covers it.

holes.name: Hegel's Rabble (Pauperismus)
holes.what: Hegel's account in the Philosophy of Right of an impoverished mass created by civil society that loses the sense of right, integrity, and honor that comes from supporting oneself by one's own work.
holes.why: Chapter 11 argues coal capitalism created the Harlan rabble that produced Boyd Crowder, and no existing slug names this specific Hegelian concept.

holes.name: Derrick Bell
holes.what: Legal scholar and founder of Critical Race Theory, who argued that racism is ordinary, structural, and advances white material and psychic interests.
holes.why: Chapter 12 analyzes Justified's racial casting entirely through Bell's Critical Race Theory, but the taxonomy lists no CRT founder.

holes.name: Interest Convergence
holes.what: Bell's thesis that reforms benefiting people of color occur only when they converge with the interests of white elite and working-class society, as in his reading of Brown v. Board of Education.
holes.why: Chapter 12 applies interest convergence and the related CRT theses (ordinariness of racism, social construction, differential racialization) as its core analytic tools, none of which the taxonomy covers.

holes.name: J.L. Austin
holes.what: Ordinary-language philosopher who distinguished justifying an act from excusing it and founded speech-act theory (performative utterances, infelicities, misfires) in How to Do Things with Words.
holes.why: Chapter 20's entire reading of 'He pulled first, I was justified', the rooftop dialogue, and Boyd's 'God made me do it' rests on Austin's justification/excuse distinction and performatives, and he is absent from the taxonomy.

holes.name: Edward Said
holes.what: Postcolonial theorist whose Orientalism showed how Western scholarship and media construct colonized peoples as exotic, savage Others to justify domination and exploitation.
holes.why: Chapter 22 builds its whole 'Appalachianism' argument - hillbilly stereotypes justifying coal exploitation - on Said's account of othering, and he is missing from the taxonomy.

holes.name: Orientalism (constructing the Other)
holes.what: Said's concept for discourses that represent a dominated people as exotic or savage Others, turning that 'knowledge' into justification for conquering and exploiting them.
holes.why: Chapter 22 transfers Orientalism to Appalachia (reality-TV hillbillies, Boyd's 'we are not your savages') and no taxonomy slug names the concept.

holes.name: Friedrich Engels
holes.what: Marx's collaborator whose Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State ties monogamy, patriarchal inheritance, and prostitution to the rise of private property.
holes.why: Chapter 26 uses Engels's property-family thesis as its central lens on Mags, Ava, and the Harlan families, but the taxonomy lists Marx without Engels.

holes.name: Oedipus Complex
holes.what: Freud's theory that sons see their fathers as rivals for the mother's affection, and that this triangle shapes character and father-son conflict.
holes.why: Chapter 27 applies the Oedipus Complex by name to Raylan-Arlo and Coover-Mags (and chapter 25 reads the failed patriarchs through the Freudian father-son lens), but the taxonomy has no Freudian slug for it.
